items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: We were partners in the Hot Record Exchange. ... Well, there's a chapter in Jasmine called New Orleans Music. Yeah. Which you did with Stephen Smith. ... Steve is much interested in New Orleans Music too, of course.

ctx.x: Did you know Fred Ramsey at, he was a graduate of Princeton I think.

Yeah, I met him in 1938. And soon after that he got the idea of, he worked for Harcourt Brace in the textbook department at that time. And talked his boss into having this anthology, Jazzmen, it turned out to be. So I had known him from around, we had what we called a hot record exchange. A friend of mine, Steve Smith, had started it in February of 36, 1936. In New York City? Yeah, in New York. He had been an artist drawing covers for, well like Wild West magazines, you know. It looked like gun smoke. The first…
Now you met all these people in New York. Yeah.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: But also another thing, while we're on the Louis subject, I remember once one year... as Steve Smith once said to me, those were the—when we were talking about a certain player.

ctx.x: Well, you could tell me how American music got started. It started at the beginning.

So anyway, to get back to the point, Gene Williams had heard these records and agreed with me too that at least Bunk showed some possibilities. You couldn't really tell much how he played, both because his lip wasn't in shape and just by himself. The type of trumpet playing that Bunk did, which was a remarkable thing, and yet by itself it wouldn't sound that effective. Bunk was hardly ever on the beat, so if you didn't hear him patting his foot and all there, you could really tell of course where the beat is, but…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: Steve Smith also organized that date.

ctx.x: He received you very ambly, though.

Yeah, very friendly. When Jelly, you see, there was that seniority business, too, that he wouldn't have, Judy, being younger, wouldn't have dared be leader. Once they wanted Jelly to record with Victor, I mean, with Decca, with Louis Armstrong, is what I'm trying to say, when they made that new Arlene's album that Louis made, and Steve Smith also organized that date. The same one that Judy was in, had a band, and the one where they makes the 219 blues. Sidney Bechet was on the date, too. And Jelly was supposed to…
Which place is that now? Music Box. The same place here.
